o: val evolves multiplicatively over rationals. Since every nums[i] is between 1 and 6, only primes 2, 3, 5 ever appear, so val is fully described by an exponent triple (a, b, c) — possibly negative — and each operation adds ±that element's exponent vector or nothing. First factor k: if k contains any prime other than 2, 3, 5, the answer is 0; otherwise record its target triple. Then count choice sequences via DP over (index, a, b, c). With n ≤ 19, exponents stay within [-19, 19], bounding states at about 20 · 39³ ≈ 1.2 million — tiny. Example [2,3,2], k=6: target (1,1,0), reachable two ways; [1,5], k=1 shows why multiply/divide by 1 both count separately (3 sequences).
k: Only primes 2, 3, 5 can occur — represent val as an exponent triple, avoiding fractions entirely.
If k has any other prime factor, the answer is immediately 0.
State space (index, a, b, c) with |exponents| ≤ n is small enough to memoize fully.

a.n: Approach 1: Memoized DFS on Exponent Triples
a.i: Recurse over indices carrying the current exponent triple; each step branches into multiply, divide, or skip. Memoization collapses overlapping states. The base case compares against k's factored triple.
s: Factor k over {2,3,5}; if a residual remains, return 0.
Precompute each nums[i]'s exponent triple (pa, pb, pc).
go(i, a, b, c) = go(i+1, a+pa, ...) + go(i+1, a-pa, ...) + go(i+1, a, b, c), with base case returning 1 iff (a,b,c) equals the target.
a.t: O(n · B³) where B = 2n+1 bounds each exponent — about 1.2M states with O(1) transitions.

a.i: Replace recursion with a rolling dictionary mapping exponent triples to counts, updated one index at a time. Each layer maps each reachable state to its three successors. Identical complexity, but avoids recursion depth concerns and makes reachability explicit.
s: For each num, build next: for each state and each of the three operations, add the count to the successor's entry.
After processing all elements, return cur.get(target, 0).
a.t: O(n · S) where S is the number of reachable states per layer (≤ 39³) — each state spawns 3 transitions.

w: Always start by factoring k — the early 0 exit is a free win and clarifies the whole design. Pitfalls: using floating-point or big rationals instead of exponent vectors (precision/perf traps), forgetting that multiply-by-1 and divide-by-1 are distinct choices (Example 3), and overflow of the count (up to 3^19 ≈ 1.16e9 — use 64-bit). Follow-ups: report the sequences themselves, allow k up to 10^18 with larger element values, or ask for the count modulo a prime.
